lessons.title: What a representative sample is
lessons.html:
What a representative sample is

When a truck brings grain to the silo, we cannot test the whole load. We take a small part of it, called a sample. The grader tests the sample to find the grade and moisture of the whole load. The farmer is paid on that grade.

A representative sample is a sample that is the same as the whole load. It has the same amount of good grain, broken grain, dust, stones, insects and moisture as the load.

Why it matters

  • If the sample is better than the load, the silo pays too much and stores poor grain with good grain.
  • If the sample is worse than the load, the farmer is paid too little. That is unfair.

Grain is not the same all through

In a truck, grain is not mixed evenly. Dust and broken grain often collect in one place. Wet grain may be at the bottom or on one side. Sometimes a load has poor grain hidden under good grain. That is why you must take grain from many places, from the top to the bottom.

Example

Bongani takes grain from only the top of a truck of maize. The top looks clean and dry. But at the bottom there is wet, mouldy maize. The grade on the ticket is wrong, and the mouldy maize goes into a good bin and spoils it. A proper sample from top to bottom would have found the problem.

Tools

  • Sampling probe (spear): a long hollow tube with openings that collects grain from top to bottom.
  • Automatic probe: a machine-driven probe at many silos.
  • Sample bucket or bag.
  • Sample divider: splits a big sample into smaller equal parts.

lessons.title: Taking, dividing and labelling the sample
lessons.html:
Taking the sample

Safety first

  • Make sure the truck engine is off and the handbrake is on before you go near it.
  • Use the sampling platform with rails. Do not walk on the load.
  • Keep away from overhead power lines with the probe.
  • Stand clear when an automatic probe is moving.
  • Wear your dust mask and safety boots.

Steps

  1. Check that the probe is clean and empty.
  2. Push the probe in at the places your site procedure shows, spread over the whole load: front, middle, back and sides.
  3. Push it all the way to the bottom each time.
  4. Close the probe, pull it out and empty it into the sample bucket.
  5. Take the number of probe samples your procedure says. Do not take fewer to save time.
  6. Look and smell. If you see insects, mould, stones, or smell something strange, tell the grader.

Dividing the sample

The sample from the truck is too big to test. Pour it through the sample divider. The divider splits it into equal parts. Keep dividing until you have the size the grader needs. Never just scoop some off the top, because that sample will not be representative.

Labelling and sealing

  • Put the sample in a clean bag or container.
  • Write on the label: truck registration, ticket number, date, time and commodity.
  • Seal it so nobody can change it.
  • Take it to the grading room quickly. Moisture can change if it waits in the sun.
  • Some samples are kept for a set time in case there is a dispute. Store them as your site says.

Never

  • Never let the driver or farmer choose where you probe.
  • Never mix samples from different trucks.

Key points

  • A representative sample is the same as the whole load.
  • Probe from top to bottom at many places in the load.
  • Divide the sample with a sample divider, never by scooping.
  • Label and seal every sample with truck and ticket details.
  • Use the platform and keep safe around trucks.
